note: Two backing tracks on one root choose two modes: Dorian over i7 and IV7, then Mixolydian over I, bVII and IV, in the same frets, so the one note that moves (the 3rd) is the lesson. Shows a key that moves (any key, 90 to 110 bpm) with the key only as {{=key}}, the chords counted the long way once as chord tokens, a {{?key}} line for another key, and a feel to reach in each block.

exercise.title: {{=key}} Dorian, then {{=key}} Mixolydian
exercise.why: Over a minor chord on the root the scale needs the minor 3rd, and over a major chord it needs the major 3rd a fret higher, so the backing track's first chord tells you which mode to play and which one note to move.

cells.text:
The backing track loops two chords of {{=key}} Dorian. {{chord:i7}} is the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}. {{chord:IV7}} is the 4th chord, built on {{4}}.
Press Play below to start the backing track. Under it is the neck with the notes of the {{=key}} Dorian scale, the root on the low E string. Improvise in it, and lean on the two ringed notes: {{b3}} makes it minor and {{6}} makes it Dorian.
Practice until you land on {{6}} each time {{chord:IV7}} comes round.

Now the backing track plays {{chord:I}}, {{chord:bVII}} and {{chord:IV}}: the 1st chord is major. Press Play below to start it. Keep your hand in the same frets and improvise in {{=key}} Mixolydian, leaning on the ringed {{3}} and {{b7}}.
When you change backing tracks, the root stays where it was and one note under your fingers moves up a fret: the minor 3rd becomes the ringed {{3}}.
{{?key}}In another key both scales sit on other frets, and the 3rd is still the one note that moves.
